## Final Project - Brief Summary

####Questions: 1.
How does the presence of the fiddler crab, Minuca pugnax, effect salt marsh stability: resistance to erosion (quantified by soil strength as a proxy) and vertical accretion?
2. Can the ribbed mussel, Guekensia demissa, offset the predicted negative effects of bioturbation of M. pugnax on marsh stability?

####Hypotheses: 
1.I predict that the bioturbative effects of M.pugnax will decrease soil strength and vertical sediment accretion. Bioturbation from the fiddler crabs will reduce belowground biomass, bulk density, and aboveground biomass contributing to a reduction in root/plant-mediated sediment trapping.

2.There are known positive effect mussels can have on plant biomass and sediment accretion in salt marshes, I hypothesize they will offset the predictive negative effects of M.pugnax for soil strength, sediment accretion and known negative effects on Spartina alterniflora aboveground biomass. Their presence can act as a mediator for sediment trapping, replacing lost sediment trapping from salt marsh grass reduction and increase soil strength through the presence of their byssal threads.

####Quick Experimental Design Background: 
In Plum Island, MA where the fiddler crab, M.pugnax is non-native to, I completed a 3-month caging study with 5 treatments: control, reference plot, crab only, mussel only, crab and mussel plot. The study was completed in a randomized block design with 8 replicates. Organisms were added to plots without fiddler crabs to minimize legacy effects and reflect a colonization event. Densities were held at 18 mussels m^-2 which reflect natural densities found throughout Plum Island. Fiddler crab densities were brought up to 85 crabs m^-2 then maintained between 50-85 m^-2 which are similar to intermediate densities found in their native range.The reference plots were the only "cages" that only had the posts and no mesh to determine if the cages themselves influenced the outcome of the results. Bioturbation is not being directly measured in this experiment, however, burrow count is a way to define burrowing activity. It is assumed that burrowing activity is continuously happening when fiddler crabs are present.

####Data collected: All data was collected at the end of the 3-month caging experiment except for live and dead stem count which was taken at the beginning and end of the experimental period.
All samples were collected in a 1/16th m\^2 plot within the cage at the end of the experiment. Soil strength used, to define erosion potential was taken at 10 cm increments to a 50 cm depth. Sediment accretion which is a factor of vertical accretion was gained by placing sediment accretion tubes for a known time thus a known mineral mass/area/time can be calculated for each treatment. An RTK was used to gain elevation (m). Mussel and crab densities were counted throughout the summer to maintain densities and gained a final 1/16th m^2 count at the end of the experiment. A ~10% sub sample of mussel height (cm) and crab carapace width (cm) were taken before placing organisms in the cages.

## Data exploration

**Use the code chunk below to load packages and the data.**

```{r setup}
#| message: false
#| error: false
library(tidyverse)
library(viridis)

data <- read.csv('Fiddler_cages_marsh_stability_working.csv') 
summary(data)
```

Need to make the NA values true NA values so the string is read as a numeric rather than chr so that I can calculate means.

```{r str data}
#| message: false
#| error: false

data <- data %>%
  mutate(sed_dep1 = as.numeric(na_if(sed_dep1, "NA")))

str(data)
```

Before making graphs I need to do some calculations. Each site there were 3 replicates of sediment deposition tubes to get a mean of sediment deposition. So I need to calculate the mean than find the deposition rate per area per time so I can compare it across sites.

```{r mean}
cols <- c("sed_dep1", "sed_dep2", "sed_dep3") #make a string to get the mean

dep_av <- rowMeans(data[cols], na.rm = TRUE) #mean while ignoring the NA

data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    sed_dep_av = (dep_av/(Area * Time_elapsed)), #sediment deposition/cm^2/day
    sed_dep_sd = sd(dep_av)/(Area * Time_elapsed) #area and time are constants between the 3 sediment deposition used for averages thus there is no variance between them. 
  )
```

Currently, mussel, crab, and stem counts are referencing a 1/16 meter squared plot.For ease of comparison, I am going to extrapolate it to a meter square density

```{r meter-squared}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    Live_count1 = Live_count1*16,
    Dead_count1 = Dead_count1*16,
    Mussel_count = Mussel_count*16,
    Burrow_count = Burrow_count*16, 
    Live_count2 = Live_count2*16,
    Dead_count2 = Dead_count2*16
  )

print(data)

```

For figure 2 I need the ss(soil strength) values in long format so that I can graph the 5 readings to depth and include a depth scale

```{r pivot_long}
pivot_long <- data[,-c(6:18,24:42)] #remove unneeded data for the graph

pivot_long <- pivot_long %>% #make table in long format with desired data
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("ss"),
    names_to = "Depth",
    names_prefix = "ss",
    values_to = "Soil_Strength"
  )

print(pivot_long)

summary_long <- pivot_long %>% #get means for simplicity of the plot
  group_by(Treatment, Depth) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(Soil_Strength), 
            se = sd(Soil_Strength),
            xmin = mean - se,
            xmax = mean + se,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Treatment = recode( #rename the Treatments
    Treatment,
    "cc" = "Crab Only",
    "mc" = "Mussel Only",
    "mcc" = "Crab & Mussel",
    "ncnc" = "Reference",
    "ncnm" = "Control"
  ))

print(summary_long)
```

**Based on your research questions, objectives, and/or testable hypotheses, develop data visualizations using ggplot2. Consider visualizations that show relationships, the distribution of the underlying data, etc. If you need inspiration, check out the [R Graph Gallery](https://r-graph-gallery.com/). For each visualization, describe your approach: what choices did you make in deciding which variables to use, plot types, etc., and why? \[2.5 pts\]**

```{r fig1}
#| message: false
#| error: false

fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x= Treatment, y = sed_dep_av, color = Elevation))+
  geom_point(size = 3)+
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Sediment Deposition (g/cm²/day)"
  )+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Crab Only", "Mussel Only", "Mussel & Crab", "Reference", "Control"))+
  scale_color_viridis()+
  theme_classic()

print(fig1)
```

For figure 1, I am looking at the different sediment deposition rates relative to each treatment. This will help to answer how the presence of the fiddler crab will effect vertical accretion and if the presence of mussels can offset the impact the fiddler crabs will have. Sediment deposition is being used to define vertical accretion. I am not trying to scale up to vertical annual accretion rates but used them as comparative values between treatments. Elevation is provided as a scale for each replicate as the cages where placed at different elevations (due to natural differences found in salt marshes). Elevation is a factor that can effect vertical accretion. Thus it is important to consider elevation compared to the sediment deposition rates calculated. For example, it makes sense that for individual treatments like the mussel only treatments, you see lower sediment deposition at replicates with higher elevation and higher sediment deposition rates in replicates with lower elevation as there is a reduction in water that is transporting sediment at higher elevations compared to lower elevations. The variance between the mussel treatment is high but that could be explained by the elevation differences similarly with the crab only plot. However the control plot also has some variance but the elevation is within a smaller range compared to other plots. I choose to do a scatter instead of a box plot because I wanted to visualize elevation at each point which I would loose this feature if I did box or violin plots.

```{r fig2}
#| message: false
#| error: false

fig2 <- ggplot(summary_long, aes(x = mean, y = Depth, color = Treatment))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line(aes(group = Treatment), orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.8)+
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)+
  facet_wrap(~ Treatment)+
  labs(
    x = "Soil Strength (kPa)",
    y = "Depth (cm)"
  )+
  scale_y_discrete(labels = c("40-50", "30-40", "20-30", "10-20", "0-10"))+
  theme_classic()

print(fig2)
```

Figure 2 hopes show relationships between treatment and soil strength at depth. This hopes to answer how differing treatments specifically the presence of fiddler crab has on erosion potential which is being measured by soil strength. Without manipulation, soil strength is expected to be highest at depths 10-20 & 20-30 as this is where a majority of the root mass from Spartina is found. I did the means of soil strength for each depth interval for each treatment. Instead of having the points all on one plot, I used facet_wrap so that I could look at each treatment individually. I reversed the depth profile using limits = rev so that visually, it was going to depth rather than the deepest core being on the top. I choose to do a line scatter as I thought this would help visually represent what is happening with soil strength at each depth. From this graph it may be interesting to see what a scatter plot of each depth looks like for each treatment.

Aboveground biomass is a factor that can influence sediment deposition, the more stems there are, the more sediments can get trapped by slowing down tidal flow, allowing particles to settle out of the water column.
The plants themselves overtime can also increase sediment accretion when they die and get buried, however this is a long - term process that was not measured by my methods. So in figure 6 I looked at how the live stem count at the end of the experimental period may have predicted sediment deposition, while having elevation shown via color gradient.
My thinking behind this was similar to other figures made in that elevation still plays a role in sediment deposition and in my model should be treated at an interaction. I choose a scatter plot again as I did not separate these by treatment as well, but would be something I would consider in my model as that would help to answer my main question about individual treatments. This was just not possible in a simple ggplot.

## Proposed analytical approach

**Considering the study design and data, and your research questions, objectives, and/or testable hypotheses, describe your proposed analytical approach. Include your response and predictor variables, type of analysis (linear regression, generalized linear regression, gam, etc.), model selection criteria, etc. Provide sufficient detail to evaluate your proposed approach in the context of your data and questions of interest. If you have questions or uncertain about anything, highlight that here as well. \[2.5 pts\]**

My response variables will be soil strength and sediment deposition where predictor variables will be stem count, presence v absence of fiddler crabs/treatment type, and elevation.
First, I will need to conduct a general linear model of some degree to evaluate if I can remove the reference plots from the rest of my analysis. To do so, I plan on conducting a t-test comparing the control to the reference plots for each of my response variables. If they are not significantly different, then I can remove the reference plots from further analysis. Here I am only testing potential caging effects on the response variables. Any reference plots with organisms in them will be removed from this analysis.

For the soil strength measurements, I plan on comparing mixed-effects models as measurements at each depth came from the same sampling location, thus they are not independent within each cage. I would plan on soil strength (at each depth) and treatment being fixed effects with each cage being a random effect. Here I would also add potentially other predictor variables like stem count to see if it strengthens the model. From the mixed-model, I would look at the ICC (inter cluster correlation coefficient) to see how the variance is explained by the random vs. fixed effects.
If the random effects is low, I plan to make a generalized linear model having depth and treatment as the fixed effects and plots acting as the independent replicates for each treatment. For each treatment I will use simple linear regressions to fit them to either linear, polynomial, or exponential curves to create models of strength vs. depth.
For all of the soil strength models I plan to compare via AIC values after looking at diagnostics from residual plots and qqplots. By singling out individual treatments via mixed-effect models by treatment, I can test which treatments are different overall from another and if treatment effects change with depth. This will help to answer if the presence or absence of fiddler crabs and mussels have an effect on erosion potential. Then, by testing the fit to linear, exponential, or polynomial models to each treatment, those models will help describe how soil strength changes with depth for each treatment and describe the pattern that is shown with depth.

Analysis of sediment deposition will answer how the presence or absence of fiddler crabs and mussels will impact vertical accretion. For this, I plan on conducting either multiple t-tests or a one-way ANOVA to compare sediment deposition between treatments if the data is normal. If the data is not normal I will look at multiple linear models to compare treatment to sediment deposition. I will also include elevation and stem count to some of these models to find the best model. Because stem count and treatment type may have an interaction, I will add an interaction term too. I will use VIF to check for any colinearity within the models I create and correct standard error if VIF is high. Using performance and predict packages in R, I will test model fit for each one then use AIC to determine which model best describes the data. If the data is non-normal I plan on moving toward generalized linear models. I do need help in figuring out which generalized linear models I should maybe look at. I know this data is on the zero to positive infinity scale but it is not continuous so I would not be able to use gamma. If I could get a suggested on what GLM I could use for this I think this is where I get stuck. I am just currently uncertain as to what to do if I don't get normal data here as I don't want to transform the raw data.
